payload.problem_addressed: Interactive game world models that autoregress appearance directly in pixel/latent space leave structured properties (pose, geometry, occlusion) to be implicitly maintained by the same generative sequence, so errors compound over long rollouts and consistency/controllability degrade.
payload.method_summary: Marionette factors the world model into three parts: a two-stage autoregressive dynamics model (compact ActionGPT for discrete per-entity actions, larger PoseGPT for continuous body pose) predicts an explicit, interpretable 276-D world state; a zero-parameter deterministic graphics bridge reconstructs metric world-space skeletons from that state via Gram-Schmidt rotation, cumulative-sum root integration, and closed-form joint placement, then rasterizes them into a pose-control video; a control-conditioned video-diffusion observation model (Wan2.2-Fun-5B DiT) renders that into photorealistic RGB, with chunk-relay for long horizons.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes explicitly modeling the evolving world state and delegating exact geometric computation to a fixed, zero-parameter renderer while letting only the neural model handle appearance, instantiated as Marionette for articulated multi-character games. It shows the predicted state is directly controllable (forcing a mismatched action stream changes joint error by 31%) and that long-horizon failures (character drift, ground penetration) are properties of the state that can be repaired by rules imposed on the state alone, without touching the observation model. Routing appearance through the predicted state costs no detectable fidelity versus an end-to-end pixel-autoregressive baseline.
key_architecture_choices: Explicit interpretable 276-D world state: per-entity root displacement, root-relative joint positions, weapon sub-state, and 6D root rotations
Two-stage dynamics: compact ActionGPT (discrete action token, ~2.5M params) + larger PoseGPT (continuous body pose, ~25M params)
Zero-parameter deterministic graphics bridge: closed-form rotation, root integration, joint placement, and rasterization with no learnable weights
Control-conditioned video-diffusion observation model (Wan2.2-Fun-5B DiT) renders pose-control video to RGB
Chunk-relay autoregressive rollout for long-horizon generation
Feasibility enforced as explicit rules/projections on the state (terrain collider, separation cap) rather than as differentiable training-time penalties
datasets: WildWorld (own released gameplay corpus: 29 monster species, 4 player characters, 4 weapon types, 5 stages)
payload.headline_results: Forcing a mismatched action stream changes root-aligned joint error by 31% (0.272->0.357m) over 48 held-out segments, showing causal control authority. A free rollout drifts characters to 21.2m apart with ground penetration in a third of frames; a terrain-collider + separation-cap rule imposed only on the state cuts penetration CFR by 66% (0.337->0.114) and holds separation at 5.1m, with no change to the observation model. Routing appearance through the predicted state costs no detectable fidelity: FVD 831 vs. 799 for recorded pose, and 831 vs. 975 against the pixel-autoregressive baseline.
claimed_advantages: Explicit metric state is directly controllable via a single token overwrite, with measurable causal authority over generated pose
Long-horizon failures (drift, penetration) are diagnosable and repairable by rules imposed on the state alone, without retraining or touching the observation model
Geometry, occlusion, and metric scale are exact by construction since a deterministic zero-parameter bridge computes them
No loss of appearance fidelity versus an end-to-end pixel-autoregressive baseline sharing the same backbone family and training footage
limitations: Dynamics model scope is single-monster in this paper; the multi-monster action vocabulary is strongly heterogeneous and scaling to it is future work
Appearance consistency across chunks still relies on the observation model's own decaying memory, propagated only through a single first-frame reference
Entities with no recorded joints (AI companions, small monsters) are unexplained by the state condition, teaching the observation model to hallucinate unstated content
Generated pose distribution differs from the ground-truth pose distribution the observation model was trained on, so results rely on generalization across that shift
A differentiable-penalty version of a state constraint was 'traded away' by the optimizer during training; only the input-feature/post-hoc-projection form of the rule held
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core offloading principle -- predict a small, structured, interpretable state with a neural model and delegate all exact geometric computation to a fixed, zero-parameter deterministic operator -- is structurally identical to hexgen's split between a neural program-emitting decoder and a deterministic mesher executor. Their finding that state infeasibility (drift, penetration) is best repaired by projecting/clamping the *interpretable intermediate state* back into a feasible region via explicit rules, rather than through differentiable training-time penalties (which the optimizer actively traded away), is directly relevant to hexgen's verifier-guided generation: it argues for post-hoc feasibility projection/repair on decoded program parameters as a more reliable lever than soft training losses alone. The two-stage decomposition (compact discrete decision model + larger continuous execution model) also mirrors a possible split between command-token selection and coordinate/parameter regression heads in hexgen's decoder.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a game-world-model paper, not CAD/geometry program synthesis -- the applicability is a mechanism-level analogy (explicit interpretable state + deterministic renderer) rather than a directly reusable component. Code is promised but not yet confirmed live at review time; the WildWorld dataset is already public. Worth revisiting once code lands, since the state-projection-as-repair idea could be prototyped directly against hexgen's frozen verifier.
dependencies_on_other_methods: Wan2.2-Fun-5B video-diffusion DiT backbone for the observation model

payload.problem_addressed: Flat (single-hop-per-layer) message passing in GNN-based mesh physics surrogates is inefficient on large, high-fidelity meshes, since long-range interactions require many hops, increasing compute, memory, and the risk of over-smoothing.
payload.method_summary: HI-MeshGraphNets (HI-MGN) replaces the flat GNN processor of MeshGraphNets with a hierarchical multiscale processor: graphs are coarsened using farthest-point sampling (FPS) plus Voronoi partitioning (preserving mesh topology without adding artificial spatial connections), message passing runs on the coarse graphs to propagate information over larger geometric distances with fewer hops, and a learned graph interpolation network projects the result back to full mesh resolution.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes a hierarchical multiscale extension of MeshGraphNets that coarsens simulation meshes via FPS and Voronoi partitioning to enable long-range message passing with fewer layers, then reconstructs fine-resolution features with a learned interpolation network. Across three structural and fluid benchmarks (2D thermoelastic, 3D nonlinear contact, 3D aerodynamic), the method improves accuracy relative to MeshGraphNets and Bi-Stride Multi-Scale GNN (BSMS-GNN) at a comparable number of message-passing blocks, while reducing training time and peak memory usage. The authors argue this demonstrates topology-aware hierarchical processing and learned coarse-to-fine interpolation as a practical route to scalable mesh-based physics surrogates.
key_architecture_choices: Hierarchical multiscale processor replacing MeshGraphNets' flat message-passing processor
Graph coarsening via farthest-point sampling (FPS) combined with Voronoi partitioning, preserving original mesh topology with no artificial spatial connections/nodes
Message passing performed on coarse graphs to cover larger geometric distances per layer
Learned graph interpolation network reconstructs fine-resolution node features from the coarse-graph output
metrics: Prediction accuracy vs. MeshGraphNets and BSMS-GNN baselines
Number of message-passing blocks (for parameter/cost matching)
payload.headline_results: HI-MGN achieves improved accuracy compared with MeshGraphNets and BSMS-GNN across three structural and fluid benchmarks, at a comparable number of message-passing blocks, while reducing training time and peak memory usage.
claimed_advantages: Improves long-range communication in mesh GNNs without adding artificial spatial connections or nodes
Reduces training time and peak memory usage versus flat and prior multiscale (BSMS-GNN) baselines
Coarsening is topology-aware, preserving the underlying mesh structure rather than introducing arbitrary graph edges
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: HI-MGN's FPS + Voronoi hierarchical coarsening and learned coarse-to-fine interpolation is a directly transferable mechanism for hexgen's graph-transformer encoder over B-rep face-adjacency graphs: if hexgen's B-rep graphs grow beyond the current ~7-15 faces (or if the mesher-side program needs to reason over finer element-level topology), the same coarsen/message-pass/interpolate recipe could extend the encoder's effective receptive field over graph hops without deepening the transformer, and it explicitly preserves topology rather than introducing artificial adjacency -- a property that matters for a domain where boundary fidelity and feature-edge capture are verifier-checked.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a physics-simulation surrogate paper (structural/fluid FEM-style meshes), not CAD B-rep or program synthesis -- relevance is via the shared substrate (graph/mesh-structured data) and multiscale message-passing mechanism, not the task itself. Extraction is based on the abstract/introduction; the numbered results tables in Sections 3-4 were not visible in the supplied text, so quantitative deltas beyond the qualitative headline claim are not confirmed here.
dependencies_on_other_methods: Builds directly on MeshGraphNets (Pfaff et al. 2020) as the flat-processor baseline
